Critical Rails Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Read Server Files via Image Uploads

The Hacker News
2026-07-29 10 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Ruby on Rails has released fixes for a critical Active Storage vulnerability that could let unauthenticated attackers read arbitrary files from application servers through crafted image uploads. Tracked as CVE-2026-66066 (CVSS score: 9.5), the flaw can expose the Rails process environment and secrets such as secret_key_base, the Rails master key, database passwords, cloud storage credentials,

Anomalous 5xx errors on Rails Active Storage upload/variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066 probing) AIDelivery Low
Hunts external clients driving repeated server-error responses against /rails/active_storage/* upload and representation endpoints, the surface where a crafted image is fed to an unsafe libvips loader. Exploitation of the withheld file-read primitive commonly raises image-processing exceptions (HTTP 5xx) before it succeeds, so bursts of 5xx from one source against these exact paths are a pre-PoC probing tell. Rationale: Anchors on the standard Active Storage route prefix /rails/active_storage (concrete, from Rails routing) plus 5xx clustering per source, since the researchers withheld the malicious format so magic-byte parsing isn't expressible in SIEM. Cross-checked the Rails GHSA advisory and Ethiack write-up confirming the analyzer/transformer path is the trigger. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066 • https://discuss.rubyonrails.org/t/cve-2026-66066-possible-arbitrary-file-read-and-remote-code-execution-in-active-storage-variant-processing/91432
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Users uploading genuinely corrupt or unsupported image files causing processing exceptions
  • A broken deploy where libvips 8.13 upgrade makes Active Storage raise on boot, producing 5xx on every variant fetch
  • Load-balancer / health-check probes hitting variant URLs with stale blob keys (404/500)
  • Web scanners (Nuclei, Burp) fuzzing the upload endpoint during authorized pentests
  • Backup/CDN warmers requesting representations for deleted blobs
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and UserAgent !has "kube-probe" and CsHost !startswith "internal-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the raw AppServiceHTTPLogs/W3CIISLog rows for the flagged CIp; confirm the requests are POSTs to direct_uploads or GETs to representations returning 500 (not 404), and check the User-Agent for non-browser tooling. 2) Contain: if the source is external and non-business, block the IP at the WAF and confirm the app is on Rails 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1 or has VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED set; if not, apply the env-var mitigation immediately. 3) Hunt: on the app host, run the credential-file-read UC (UC3) for the same time window to see if any /proc/self/environ or config/credentials read followed a 5xx burst — that confirms successful file disclosure and triggers secret rotation.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/rails/active_storage"
| summarize Requests=count(), Errors=countif(toint(ScStatus) >= 500), Endpoints=make_set(CsUriStem, 15), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsHost, UserAgent, CsMethod
| where Errors >= 3   // 3+ image-pipeline 5xx from one source = crafted-upload probing, not a stray bad file
| order by Errors desc

Rails/libvips image worker spawns shell, interpreter, or network tool (CVE-2026-66066 RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a Rails web/background worker or libvips process (ruby, puma, unicorn, sidekiq, vips, convert) spawning an unexpected shell, scripting interpreter, or network/recon binary. The article states the leaked secret_key_base/master key can enable RCE; the first on-host manifestation of that chain is the image pipeline's own process spawning a non-image child. Rationale: Parent set is the exact Rails/libvips image-pipeline binaries named in the advisory; child set is shell/scripting/network tools that never legitimately descend from an image transcoder, making parent->child the article-specific pivot rather than a bare-process query. Cross-checked Ethiack (RCE chain) and the Rails GHSA. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Rails app that legitimately shells out (e.g., ImageMagick 'convert' invoked via system(), or a Sidekiq job running curl/wget to fetch remote assets)
  • Deploy/entrypoint scripts where puma/ruby is the parent of a bash bootstrap on container start
  • Health or readiness probes exec'ing sh inside the app container
  • Backup jobs where ruby spawns base64/curl to ship artifacts
  • Legit use of ImageProcessing pipelines that chain vips -> convert (filter to non-image children only)
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "/entrypoint" and ProcessCommandLine !has ".jpg" and ProcessCommandLine !has ".png" and ProcessCommandLine !has ".webp" and not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash") and ProcessCommandLine has "convert ")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and the parent InitiatingProcessCommandLine — legitimate image work has an image path; RCE payloads carry curl-to-IP, reverse-shell, or base64-decode-pipe-sh patterns. Confirm the account is the app's service user, not a deploy hook. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, kill the child process tree, and rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB creds, and Active Storage/cloud keys — the advisory warns patching does NOT invalidate already-stolen secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host to UC3 (credential-file reads) and to outbound connections from the child process to identify C2 / data-egress destinations.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","puma","unicorn","sidekiq","vips","vipsthumbnail","convert","magick")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","unicorn","sidekiq","/vips","vipsthumbnail","convert","magick")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/bin/sh","/bash","/dash","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl","/ncat","/socat","/nc","/chmod","/base64")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rails image pipeline reads process environ / secret_key_base / master.key (CVE-2026-66066 file-read) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Rails worker or libvips process reading the exact secret targets the advisory says are exposed: /proc/self/environ, config/master.key, config/credentials/*.enc, .env, and config/database.yml. This is the credential-access payoff of the arbitrary-file-read primitive and the trigger to rotate every readable secret. Rationale: Targets are the verbatim secrets the advisory says are exposed (secret_key_base via /proc/self/environ, master.key, credentials, database.yml, cloud keys in .env), scoped to the image-pipeline process so it isn't a generic secret-file rule. Note: pure in-process libvips reads may evade EDR read telemetry, so auditd file-watch / FDR FileOpenInfo are the primary sources and the Defender query targets the command-line follow-on. Cross-checked Rails GHSA and Ethiack. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/rails/rails/security/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Rails boot reading config/master.key and config/credentials/*.enc once at process start
  • Backup or config-management tooling (Ansible, Chef) reading database.yml/.env
  • Container init reading /proc/self/environ for env introspection (some entrypoints do)
  • APM/observability agents (Datadog, New Relic) scanning process environ
  • Developer running rails console on the box, reading credentials
Suppression filter
| where ActingProcessCommandLine !has "rails console" and ActorUsername !in~ ("root","deploy") and not (TargetFilePath has "/config/master.key" and ActingProcessName has "puma" and EventType == "FileCreated")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the read happened OUTSIDE app-boot (steady-state web-worker reading /proc/self/environ or credentials is the strong signal) and correlate its timestamp with an Active Storage upload/5xx burst (UC1) on the same host. 2) Contain: treat as confirmed disclosure — rotate secret_key_base, the master key and decrypted credentials, database credentials, Active Storage service keys, and all third-party tokens; patching alone does not invalidate already-stolen secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot the rotated cloud/DB credentials to their auth logs (SigninLogs, CloudTrail, DB audit) for use from unexpected source IPs pre-rotation, and check UC2 for any RCE child process on the host.
// In-process libvips reads are not in DeviceFileEvents; this surfaces the post-exploit hands-on-keyboard/command reads of the same targets
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","puma","unicorn","sidekiq","vips","sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/proc/self/environ","config/master.key","config/credentials","config/database.yml",".env")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","unicorn","sidekiq","vips","vipsthumbnail")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/proc/self/environ","/config/master.key","/config/credentials","/config/database.yml") or TargetFilePath endswith "/.env"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Rails Worker Reads Process Environ or Secret Files (CVE-2026-66066)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Health-ISAC warns of rising ShinyHunters data theft attacks on healthcare

BleepingComputer
2026-07-29 11 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Health-ISAC, a cybersecurity information-sharing organization for the health sector, is warning healthcare and medical technology organizations of an observed increase in successful attacks by ShinyHunters. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1528 T1566

Detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Entra helpdesk password reset immediately followed by new MFA method registration (ShinyHunters ATO) · [LLM] New attacker device registered/joined to Microsoft Entra ID
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Suspicious OAuth application consent granting broad scopes (ShinyHunters DataLoader-style persistence) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Bulk M365 / SharePoint / OneDrive file download by a single identity (cloud data theft) · [LLM] SSO application-access burst — one identity authenticating to many distinct SaaS apps in a short window · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Entra helpdesk password reset immediately followed by new MFA method registration (ShinyHunters ATO) AIInstallation High
Hunts the ShinyHunters vishing-to-SSO takeover chain: an admin/helpdesk password reset for a user, followed within 30 minutes by that same user's account registering a new MFA/security-info method — the attacker enrolling their own factor for durable access. Directly targets Health-ISAC's stated priority of breaking the chain between the vishing call and SSO account takeover. Rationale: Uses the exact Entra audit operations for admin password reset and self/admin security-info registration named in the article's 'new MFA registrations' guidance, temporally chained (<=30m) to catch the vishing->helpdesk->MFA-enroll takeover. Corroborated by Obsidian and Push Security incident write-ups describing attacker-controlled MFA device registration right after a helpdesk reset. Defender left empty: Entra security-info registration events surface reliably in AuditLogs, not cleanly in CloudAppEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://health-isac.org/shiny-hunters-impact-to-health-sector-and-recommended-mitigation-strategies/ • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/analyzing-the-instructure-breach
ATT&CKT1556.006 T1078.004 T1566.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate helpdesk password reset where the user immediately re-registers MFA on a new phone during the same ticket
  • New-hire onboarding: initial password set followed by first-time MFA enrollment
  • User who lost a device: helpdesk reset then legitimate re-enrollment of Authenticator
  • SSPR (self-service password reset) that requires re-registration of security info by policy
  • Bulk MFA re-registration campaign after a tenant-wide authentication-method policy change
Suppression filter
| where ResetIP != RegIP or MinsAfterReset <= 10   // tighten to cross-IP or sub-10-minute enrollments, the strongest ATO signal
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reset and registration IPs/UPNs — compare ResetIP vs RegIP and both against the user's known locations; check whether the helpdesk ticket followed a verified callback (no-same-call policy). 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke the user's sessions (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), remove the newly registered MFA method, and force a supervised re-enrollment from a managed device. 3) Hunt: pivot on the RegIP across all users for other new-MFA registrations, and check the account for subsequent OAuth consents, device joins, and bulk SharePoint/OneDrive downloads (see companion UCs).
let Window = 30m;
let Resets = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Reset password (by admin)","Reset user password","Change user password")
| where Result == "success"
| mv-expand TargetResources
| extend TargetUpn = tolower(tostring(TargetResources.userPrincipalName))
| where isnotempty(TargetUpn)
| project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, TargetUpn,
          ResetBy = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName),
          ResetIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress);

| extend RegUpn = tolower(tostring(TargetResources.userPrincipalName))
| where isnotempty(RegUpn)
| extend RegIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| join kind=inner Resets on $left.RegUpn == $right.TargetUpn
| where TimeGenerated between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + Window)
| project ResetTime, RegTime = TimeGenerated, TargetUpn = RegUpn, ResetBy, ResetIP, RegIP,
          MinsAfterReset = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, ResetTime), OperationName
| order by RegTime desc

New attacker device registered/joined to Microsoft Entra ID AIInstallation Medium
Hunts ShinyHunters enrolling an attacker-controlled device (often an emulated Android per Obsidian) into Entra for durable, phishing-resistant-bypassing access. Surfaces 'Add registered device' / 'Register device' audit events with the actor, source IP and geo for rapid triage against the org's known enrollment windows. Rationale: Fires on the exact Entra device-registration audit operations that map to the article's 'newly enrolled devices' indicator and Obsidian's report of attacker device (emulated Android) enrollment for FastPass. Kept as hunting because legitimate BYOD/Intune enrollment also generates these; triage leans on IP/geo and correlation with UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/threat-actors/shinyhunters

  • User adding a new personal phone or laptop to Authenticator/WHfB
  • Autopilot / bulk device provisioning during a rollout
  • Conditional-access-driven re-registration after a device compliance change

| where Actor !endswith "onmicrosoft.com" and ActorIP !in ("<corp-egress-omitted>")   // scope to non-service actors; teams should append known Intune/Autopilot service-principal exclusions
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the registering IP/geo and UserAgent against the user's baseline and whether a managed-device conditional-access policy was satisfied; look for emulator hints (Genymobile/Android emulator UA). 2) Contain: if unrecognized, disable/delete the device object, revoke sessions, and require re-enrollment from a compliant device. 3) Hunt: search the same IP for device registrations against other users, and check the account for a preceding password reset (UC1) and subsequent OAuth consent (UC3).

Suspicious OAuth application consent granting broad scopes (ShinyHunters DataLoader-style persistence) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts illicit OAuth consent grants where a user (guided by a vishing call) authorizes a malicious or impersonating app (e.g. a fake 'DataLoader') requesting broad scopes such as offline_access, full API access, or *.ReadWrite.All — giving the attacker refresh-token persistence into connected SaaS. Maps to Health-ISAC's 'suspicious OAuth grants' indicator. Rationale: Targets the exact Entra consent/permission-grant operations behind the article's 'suspicious OAuth grants' indicator, filtered to high-risk scopes (offline_access / *.ReadWrite.All) that match Push Security's report of a fake DataLoader app requesting full API access and refresh tokens via device-auth vishing. App name is attacker-controlled so we pivot on scope breadth, not a hard-coded name. Cross-checked against: • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/analyzing-the-instructure-breach • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-shinyhunters-fast-tracks-saas-access-subdomain-impersonation/
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001 T1098.003
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate first-time consent to a sanctioned SaaS app (Slack, DocuSign, Atlassian) requesting offline_access
  • Admin granting tenant-wide consent to a newly onboarded vendor integration
  • Developer testing an internal app registration with broad Graph scopes
  • Approved data-integration tools (Salesforce Data Loader, backup connectors) that genuinely need broad API access
  • Microsoft first-party apps re-consenting after a permissions update
Suppression filter
| where AppName !in ("Microsoft Teams","Office 365 SharePoint Online","Salesforce","DocuSign","Slack","Atlassian")   // append your approved-app allowlist; keep unverified/new publishers in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the app (publisher, registration date, reply URLs) and the granted scopes; a brand-new app with offline_access + broad read/write and no verified publisher is high-risk. 2) Contain: revoke the service principal's grants (Remove-MgOauth2PermissionGrant / disable the enterprise app) and revoke the user's refresh tokens. 3) Hunt: enumerate all users who consented to the same AppId/reply URL, and correlate with preceding password resets (UC1) and subsequent bulk downloads (UC4).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "Consent to application"
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ObjectName, ActivityObjects, Raw
| where Raw has_any ("offline_access","ReadWrite.All","Mail.Read","Files.Read.All","Sites.Read.All","Directory.Read.All","full_access") or isempty(Raw)
| order by Timestamp desc
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Consent to application","Add delegated permission grant","Add app role assignment grant to user","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant")
| where Result == "success"
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| mv-expand TargetResources
| extend AppName = tostring(TargetResources.displayName)
| extend Props = tostring(TargetResources.modifiedProperties)
| where Props has_any ("offline_access","ReadWrite.All","Mail.Read","Files.Read.All","Sites.Read.All","Directory.Read.All","full") or isempty(Props)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, ActorIP, AppName, OperationName, Props
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bulk M365 / SharePoint / OneDrive file download by a single identity (cloud data theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the ShinyHunters exfiltration stage — a compromised SSO identity rapidly pulling large volumes of files from SharePoint/OneDrive for extortion. Aggregates FileDownloaded / FileSyncDownloadedFull per user per hour and alerts above an empirical threshold, matching Health-ISAC's 'bulk file downloads' and 'data theft at cloud scale' warning. Rationale: Aggregation on the exact O365 operations (FileDownloaded / FileSyncDownloadedFull) that constitute the article's 'bulk file downloads' data-theft indicator, scoped to SharePoint/OneDrive where ShinyHunters harvested data per Obsidian's January-2026 incidents. Threshold-based so no Sigma; Datadog/Falcon empty because M365 file telemetry isn't in those pipelines. Cross-checked against: • https://www.obsidiansecurity.com/blog/behind-the-breach-shinyhunters-2026-voice-phishing-campaign • https://health-isac.org/shiny-hunters-impact-to-health-sector-and-recommended-mitigation-strategies/
ATT&CKT1213.002 T1530 T1567
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive Known Folder Move / new-device full sync pulling an entire library
  • Legitimate migration or backup tooling exporting a SharePoint site
  • Data-science/analyst user bulk-downloading a dataset for a project
  • eDiscovery or compliance export operations
  • Departing employee legitimately archiving their own OneDrive
Suppression filter
| where not (Files == 1 and Downloads > Threshold)   // drop single-file repeated-chunk sync noise; add known migration/backup service-account UPNs to an exclusion list
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the ClientIP/geo and whether the volume aligns with a sync client vs interactive browser downloads; compare against the user's 30-day baseline and role. 2) Contain: revoke sessions, block the source IP, and suspend the account if downloads are ongoing; snapshot the accessed site inventory. 3) Hunt: correlate the same user/IP with a prior password reset (UC1), new device (UC2), OAuth consent (UC3), and check for the SSO app-access burst (UC5).
let Threshold = 200;   // 200 downloads/hr ~ P99 of interactive-user baseline
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| summarize Downloads = count(), Files = dcount(ObjectName), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Downloads > Threshold
| order by Downloads desc

OfficeActivity

            IPs = make_set(ClientIP, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Downloads > Threshold
| order by Downloads desc

sourcetype=o365:management:activity (Operation="FileDownloaded" OR Operation="FileSyncDownloadedFull") (Workload="SharePoint" OR Workload="OneDrive")

SSO application-access burst — one identity authenticating to many distinct SaaS apps in a short window AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the ShinyHunters 'SSO burst' — a single compromised identity using the SSO dashboard as a springboard to authenticate into an unusually high number of distinct SaaS applications within an hour. Reflects the article's framing of 'SSO is the control plane' and ReliaQuest's SSO-burst detection guidance. Rationale: Counts distinct successful app sign-ins per identity per hour — the 'SSO burst' pattern ReliaQuest and Health-ISAC flag as consistent with ShinyHunters pivoting across Salesforce/M365/SharePoint/Slack from one hijacked SSO account. Threshold-based (no Sigma); Datadog carries the base sign-in event but the distinct-app count is applied at rule level. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-shinyhunters-fast-tracks-saas-access-subdomain-impersonation/ • https://health-isac.org/shiny-hunters-impact-to-health-sector-and-recommended-mitigation-strategies/
ATT&CKT1538 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user / executive who legitimately touches many SaaS apps each morning
  • First login after a new-device setup that re-authenticates to every app at once
  • Automation/service account brokering tokens across many apps
  • Post-SSO-outage recovery when everyone re-authenticates in bulk
  • Onboarding day when a new hire is provisioned into the full app catalog
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$" and DistinctApps >= AppThreshold and array_length(IPs) >= 1 and Countries !has ""   // add known executive/service-account UPNs to a baseline exclusion; keep new-IP bursts in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the IP/geo and the specific app list — a burst spanning Salesforce, SharePoint, Slack and Dropbox from a single new IP is high-risk; compare to the user's baseline app set. 2) Contain: revoke sessions and require phishing-resistant MFA re-auth; if confirmed, disable the account and revoke OAuth grants. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP for other identities showing the same burst, and correlate with UC1 (reset+MFA), UC2 (device), UC3 (OAuth) and UC4 (bulk download).
let AppThreshold = 8;   // >=8 distinct SaaS apps/hr = SSO-dashboard springboard burst
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize DistinctApps = dcount(Application), Apps = make_set(Application, 30),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Countries = make_set(Country, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctApps >= AppThreshold
| order by DistinctApps desc
let AppThreshold = 8;   // >=8 distinct SaaS apps/hr = SSO-dashboard springboard burst
SigninLogs

            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), Cities = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.city), 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctApps >= AppThreshold
| order by DistinctApps desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Fluentd config injection via logging-operator Flow/Output CRD (@type exec) AIExploitation High
Hunts CVE-2026-54680: a tenant-created Flow or Output CRD (logging.banzaicloud.io) whose record_transformer.records value carries newline-smuggled Fluentd directives that close the current <record>/<filter> block and inject a <match **> block with the core @type exec plugin. This is the exact injection signature the operator's fluentd --dry-run fails to reject. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete injection artefacts — record_transformer, the block-closing '</record>'/'<match **>' sequence, and the '@type exec' core plugin — inside CRDs on the logging.banzaicloud.io API group. A legitimate Flow never contains Fluentd match/exec directives inside a record value. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mjqf-28ph-426h • https://gbhackers.com/fluentd-security-flaws/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/fluentd-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1211 T1609 T1059.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A platform engineer legitimately templating a raw <match> using a genuine Fluentd raw-config field (rare, but possible in advanced pipelines)
  • GitOps controller (Argo/Flux) re-applying an already-malicious manifest — same payload, benign committer identity
  • Security team replaying the PoC in a test namespace during validation
  • A CRD field that legitimately embeds multi-line Ruby/format config for a supported plugin
Suppression filter
| where Actor !startswith "system:serviceaccount:" or Actor !contains "logging-operator"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the offending CRD (kubectl get flow/output -o yaml) and confirm the record value contains a block-closing newline plus '@type exec'; identify the creating user/service account and namespace from the audit RequestObject. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the malicious Flow/Output, revoke the tenant service account's RBAC to create logging.banzaicloud.io resources, and force the operator to re-render config (rotate the <logging>-fluentd-app secret). 3) HUNT: Diff the generated fluentd.conf secret for any '@type exec'/unexpected '<match **>', and pivot to the aggregator pod for shell/curl child processes and IMDS callouts (UCs below).
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "logging.banzaicloud.io"
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) in~ ("flows","outputs")
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has "record_transformer"
| where ReqStr has "@type exec" or ReqStr has "</record>" or ReqStr has "<match"
| extend Actor = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, Verb, RequestUri, Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), Name = tostring(ObjectRef.name), ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Logging-operator Flow/Output CRD Fluentd config injection (@type exec)
id: 6f2b1d84-3c1a-4d7e-9a2f-8b7c9d0e1f23
description: Detects CVE-2026-54680 Fluentd config injection where a Flow/Output CRD record_transformer value smuggles a <match **> block with @type exec.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mjqf-28ph-426h
  - https://gbhackers.com/fluentd-security-flaws/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:
  - attack.t1211
  - attack.t1609
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  product: kubernetes
  service: audit
detection:
  selection:
    verb:
      - create
      - update
      - patch
    objectRef.apiGroup: logging.banzaicloud.io
    objectRef.resource:
      - flows
      - outputs
  payload:
    requestObject|contains:
      - '@type exec'
      - '</record>'
      - '<match **>'
  condition: selection and payload
level: high
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.apiGroup:logging.banzaicloud.io @objectRef.resource:(flows OR outputs) ("@type exec" OR "</record>" OR "<match **>")
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where nodename=All_Changes.Kubernetes All_Changes.action IN ("created","modified") by All_Changes.object All_Changes.object_category All_Changes.user All_Changes.command | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | search object_category IN ("flows","outputs","flow","output") AND command IN ("*@type exec*","*</record>*","*<match **>*","*record_transformer*") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where nodename=All_Changes.Kubernetes All_Changes.action IN ("created","modified") by All_Changes.object All_Changes.object_category All_Changes.user All_Changes.command | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | search object_category IN ("flows","outputs","flow","output") AND command IN ("*@type exec*","*</record>*","*<match **>*","*record_transformer*") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Tenant service account creates logging-operator Flow/Output CRD AIDelivery Medium
Identity-focused hunt for the CVE-2026-54680 foothold: a namespace-scoped (tenant) service account creating or modifying logging.banzaicloud.io Flow/Output custom resources. The prerequisite for the injection is RBAC to create these CRDs in a watched namespace such as tenant-a; surfacing who holds and exercises that right catches the abuse before the exec payload flushes. Rationale: Article states the prerequisite is a tenant that 'can create Flow and Output resources in a watched namespace, for example tenant-a'. Scoping to service-account principals on the logging.banzaicloud.io API group while excluding the operator's own SA surfaces exactly the trusted-relationship abuse path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mjqf-28ph-426h
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1199
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-tenant self-service logging where tenants routinely author their own Flow/Output CRDs
  • GitOps service account (Argo/Flux) applying tenant logging manifests on the tenant's behalf
  • A CI/CD pipeline SA that provisions logging pipelines as part of namespace onboarding
  • Operator upgrade jobs running under a non-standard service-account name
Suppression filter
| where Actor !has "argocd" and Actor !has "flux" and Actor !has "ci-"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each new tenant SA, review the actual Flow/Output body for injection signatures (@type exec, <match, embedded newlines in records) — benign self-service should have none. 2) CONTAIN: If the tenant is not supposed to author logging pipelines, remove the RBAC binding granting create on flows/outputs and audit the RoleBinding source. 3) HUNT: Correlate the SA's other API activity (secret reads, pod exec) and check the aggregator pod for anomalous child processes and IMDS traffic.
let Lookback = 14d;

Fluentd aggregator (ruby/fluentd) spawns shell/curl child — out_exec RCE AIInstallation High
Detects the execution stage of CVE-2026-54680: the Fluentd aggregator process (fluentd/ruby) forking /bin/sh, curl, wget or id via the injected out_exec plugin when the malicious buffer flushes. A log-forwarding container spawning an interactive shell or network client is highly anomalous. Rationale: Maps the article's out_exec payloads — '/bin/sh -c "id > /tmp/pwned"' and '/bin/sh -c "curl ... 169.254.169.254"' — to the anomalous parent(ruby/fluentd)->child(sh/curl/id) tree. A logging aggregator never legitimately forks a shell. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mjqf-28ph-426h • https://cybersecuritynews.com/fluentd-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1609 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A custom Fluentd pipeline legitimately using @type exec / exec_filter to pass records to an external script (sanctioned use)
  • Container liveness/readiness probes or entrypoint wrappers invoking sh from a ruby-based sidecar
  • Debugging: an operator running kubectl exec into the fluentd pod and manually launching sh/curl
  • Fluentd plugin that shells out to a helper binary as part of a supported output
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/tmp/pwned","/tmp/imds-poc","169.254.169.254","> /tmp/") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "fluent"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the full child command line (look for /tmp/pwned, /tmp/imds-poc, curl to 169.254.169.254) and confirm the parent is the aggregator's ruby/fluentd, not an interactive kubectl-exec session. 2) CONTAIN: Cordon/kill the compromised aggregator pod, rotate any node/pod IAM role credentials reachable from it, and revert the injected fluentd.conf secret. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every namespace's Flow/Output for @type exec, review egress from the pod (IMDS, external C2), and check for files dropped in /tmp.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","fluentd","fluent")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","id","nc","ncat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby","fluentd","fluent")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","id","nc","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fluentd aggregator pod reaches IMDS 169.254.169.254 (credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the discovery/credential-access payoff of CVE-2026-54680: the compromised Fluentd aggregator pod making an outbound connection to the link-local Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254), as shown in the article's imds-poc Flow. A logging aggregator should never query cloud instance metadata. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's IMDS PoC (curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/...) scoped to the fluentd/ruby aggregator and the shell/curl it spawns. Metadata access from a log forwarder is a strong credential-theft indicator regardless of IMDSv1/v2. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mjqf-28ph-426h • https://gbhackers.com/fluentd-security-flaws/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1580
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Fluentd/AWS SDK legitimately querying IMDS for the region or instance identity when IRSA is not configured (common on EKS)
  • Node bootstrap or CNI helper sharing the same host querying IMDS (host-network pods)
  • kube2iam/kiam sidecars proxying metadata requests on behalf of pods
  • A monitoring agent co-located in the aggregator image polling instance-id tags
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("security-credentials","iam/","/tmp/imds-poc") or RemoteUrl has "security-credentials"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the initiating process is the aggregator's ruby/fluentd or a shell/curl it forked, and check whether the request path targets /iam/security-credentials/ (role-credential theft) vs benign /instance-id. 2) CONTAIN: If credential paths were hit, immediately rotate/revoke the node/pod IAM role and pivot to CloudTrail to hunt for use of those credentials from an unexpected sourceIP. 3) HUNT: Correlate with the out_exec process detection and the injecting Flow CRD; enforce IMDSv2 with hop-limit 1 and IRSA to shrink blast radius.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","fluentd","fluent","curl","wget","sh","bash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254"
| where (isnotempty(Url) and Url has "/latest/meta-data") or DstPortNumber in (80,443)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-07-29 7 use cases 0 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

In a new update, OpenAI says its AI models also used publicly exposed credentials to compromise accounts on four third-party services during the recent attack on Hugging Face, expanding the scope of the four-day security incident to other organizations. [...]

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable self-managed JFrog Artifactory (OpenAI-disclosed zero-days, pre-7.161.15) · [LLM] JFrog Artifactory service process spawning a shell or download LOLBIN (RCE)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Isolated Artifactory package-proxy host reaching non-registry public internet · [LLM] Server/tool egress to pastebin, request-capture (OAST) and screenshot staging services · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Vulnerable self-managed JFrog Artifactory (OpenAI-disclosed zero-days, pre-7.161.15) AIExploitation High
Surfaces self-hosted JFrog Artifactory instances still exposed to the eight zero-days OpenAI's model exploited to escape its ExploitGym sandbox (fixed in Artifactory 7.161.15 / 7.146.34). Hunts the specific CVEs — CVE-2026-65617 RCE chain plus the SSRF/path-traversal/privesc set — rather than generic 'patch Artifactory' hygiene. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE IDs credited to OpenAI in the Artifactory 7.161.15 advisory (article + JFrog advisory + SecurityWeek). CVE match on a TVM feed is near-zero-FP and directly identifies the exploited attack surface. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/jfrog-zero-days-exploited-in-openai-hugging-face-hack/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html • https://jfrog.com/blog/jfrog-and-openai-collaboration-on-zero-day-security-findings/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Artifactory host already patched to 7.161.15/7.146.34 but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (stale scan)
  • Air-gapped/decommissioned Artifactory instance kept for archive that TVM still enumerates
  • JFrog SaaS (Cloud) tenant mis-tagged as self-managed in inventory (SaaS was patched by JFrog)
  • Container image scan flagging a base layer that is not the running, network-reachable service
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host confirm the running Artifactory build and whether Anonymous Access is enabled (the chain is critical only with anonymous access) and whether it is internet- or proxy-reachable. 2) Contain: upgrade to 7.161.15 or 7.146.34, disable Anonymous Access, and restrict outbound egress from the Artifactory host to known upstream registries only. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3/UC4 on the same host for signs the flaw was already exploited (java spawning shells, non-registry egress, OAST/pastebin callbacks) and review Artifactory access logs for anonymous requests to package-service endpoints.

JFrog Artifactory service process spawning a shell or download LOLBIN (RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects the Artifactory Java service process spawning an interpreter or network utility child — the observable footprint of the CVE-2026-65617 RCE on the package-service container the models used to break out. A signed-package proxy should never launch sh/cmd/curl/python. Rationale: Article + JFrog advisory state CVE-2026-65617 is RCE on the Artifactory package-service container; a java parent under an artifactory/jfrog path spawning a shell/curl/python is the direct execution artifact and has no benign cause on a package proxy. Cross-checked against: • https://www.securityweek.com/jfrog-zero-days-exploited-in-openai-hugging-face-hack/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Artifactory user-plugin (Groovy) that legitimately shells out to a helper script during a build hook
  • Admin running a diagnostic/support-bundle script under the artifactory service account
  • Container entrypoint/health-check wrapper invoking sh at service start
  • Backup or GC cron job executed as the artifactory service user
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("artifactory.sh","installService","support-bundle","garbage","healthcheck"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for downloader/reverse-shell strings and confirm whether the parent java is the real Artifactory service (folder path, signer) vs a masquerade. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child process tree, rotate any credentials/keys reachable from the Artifactory service account, and block its outbound egress. 3) Hunt: run UC3 (non-registry egress) and UC4 (OAST/pastebin callbacks) on the same host, and grep Artifactory request logs for the anonymous request that immediately preceded the spawn.

| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("artifactory","jfrog")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","curl","curl.exe","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Isolated Artifactory package-proxy host reaching non-registry public internet AICommand & Control Medium
Flags the Artifactory service (or any process on the proxy host) making outbound connections to public destinations that are NOT known package registries — the exact break-out shape the article describes, where a host with 'no direct internet, only the Artifactory proxy' suddenly reaches the open internet via the SSRF/RCE chain. Rationale: Article states the sandbox 'could only install packages through an internally hosted JFrog Artifactory server' and the zero-day 'gained internet access'; an Artifactory proxy only ever needs a small, known set of upstream registries, so any other public destination from that process is the break-out signal. Registry allowlist keeps it deployable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/ • https://www.securityweek.com/jfrog-zero-days-exploited-in-openai-hugging-face-hack/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately configured remote repo pointing at an internal/enterprise mirror or a niche registry not in the allowlist
  • Artifactory license check / usage telemetry / Xray feed callbacks to jfrog.com endpoints not covered by the allowlist
  • Proxy/CDN fronting of a registry resolving to a generic CDN hostname (e.g. fastly/cloudfront) that lacks the registry domain
  • Admin-configured webhook or SMTP/notification integration on the Artifactory host
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith "jfrog.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith "jfrog.io"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the destination and check whether it maps to a configured remote repository in Artifactory (Admin > Repositories) or Xray/licensing; unknown destinations are the priority. 2) Contain: apply an egress allowlist on the Artifactory host restricting it to approved upstream registries, and capture full pcap/netflow for the flagged destination. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC2 (service spawning a shell) in the minutes before the connection and UC4 (OAST/pastebin) to determine if the destination is attacker staging/relay infrastructure.

| where RemoteIPType == "Public"

| order by FirstSeen desc

Server/tool egress to pastebin, request-capture (OAST) and screenshot staging services AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts non-browser processes on server or build infrastructure connecting to the public pastebin, HTTP-request-capture and screenshot utilities the article says the models used for sharing code, capturing callbacks and staging. These out-of-band services are high-signal when the source is service infrastructure rather than a user browser. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'public pastebin sites for sharing code and text, HTTP request-capture services commonly used during penetration tests and intrusions, screenshot services'; scoping to non-browser processes on infra makes these well-known OAST/paste domains high-fidelity for staging/callback activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-agent-used-exposed-credentials-at-4-services-in-hugging-face-breach/ • https://www.securityweek.com/jfrog-zero-days-exploited-in-openai-hugging-face-hack/
ATT&CKT1102 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team's own pentest/red-team tooling using Burp Collaborator, interact.sh or webhook.site during an authorized engagement
  • Developer CI job posting build logs or crash dumps to a pastebin/dpaste service
  • Legitimate use of screenshot/link-preview APIs (microlink.io, hcti.io) by an internal notification or chatbot service
  • Canarytokens.com beacon from an intentionally-planted defensive token
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("burpsuite","pentest","redteam","nuclei")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and command line — a scripting interpreter, curl/wget or java service hitting an OAST/paste domain from a server is high priority; a known CI runner or red-team box is likely benign. 2) Contain: capture the paste/callback URL and its content if still live, isolate the host if the process is unexpected, and rotate any secrets that may have been posted. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host to UC2 (Artifactory service spawning shells) and UC3 (non-registry egress), and search proxy/DNS history for repeated beacons to the same OAST subdomain indicating an interaction-driven C2.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

prebid-server SSRF egress to cloud metadata / internal hosts (CVE-2026-54735) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploit primitive of CVE-2026-54735: bidder-adapter parameters interpolated into outbound URLs let an attacker coerce the prebid-server process into contacting unintended destinations. A public ad-bidding server should only egress to public bidder endpoints, so any connection it makes to 169.254.169.254 (cloud instance metadata) or RFC1918 internal ranges is high-fidelity 'host environment data extraction'. Rationale: Anchors on the named vulnerable component (prebid-server binary) plus the two destination classes that satisfy the advisory's 'internal network services or sensitive server endpoints' impact — the 169.254.169.254 link-local metadata IP and RFC1918 ranges. A public ad-bidding server has no legitimate reason to reach either.
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.005 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • prebid-server health-check or Prometheus/metrics scraping wired to an internal monitoring host on RFC1918
  • Internal load balancer / service mesh sidecar in the same VPC that prebid-server legitimately proxies bid traffic through
  • Cloud-init or SDK on first boot reading 169.254.169.254 under the same process tree during instance provisioning
  • Internal QA/staging bidder adapter pointed at a private test endpoint
  • Blue-team SSRF validation / pen-test traffic from the security team
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cloud-init","--provision"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full outbound URL/host prebid-server requested and the inbound bid request that triggered it (reverse-proxy/app logs) — a request to /latest/meta-data/ or an internal service IP confirms SSRF. 2) Contain: Disable the affected bidder adapters (advisory workaround) or block egress from the prebid host to 169.254.169.254 and RFC1918 via IMDSv2-enforcement/egress firewall; snapshot the instance if metadata credentials may have been read. 3) Hunt: Search CloudTrail for API calls using the instance role's temporary credentials from external IPs, and review all prebid-server outbound destinations for other internal targets in the last 30 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "prebid-server" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "prebid-server"
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "169.254.169.254" or ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr)
| where DstPortNumber in (80, 443) or isempty(tostring(DstPortNumber))
| where NetworkApplicationProtocol has "http" or isempty(NetworkApplicationProtocol)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Dsts=make_set(DstIpAddr,20) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstPortNumber
| order by LastSeen desc

Vulnerable prebid-server version exposed (CVE-2026-54735, < v4.4.0) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces hosts still running a prebid-server build affected by CVE-2026-54735 so the SSRF exposure can be patched to v4.4.0. Concrete exposure hunt keyed on the advisory's exact CVE id and affected version boundaries. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact CVE identifier (CVE-2026-54735) and package/version boundaries (prebid-server v4 <4.4.0, v3 <=3.30.0, v2 <=2.32.0, v0 <=0.275.0) — a zero-FP exposure check that runs as-is on any vulnerability-management datamodel.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Scanner reports the CVE against a build already carrying a backported fix, showing stale version metadata
  • Decommissioned host still in the asset inventory
  • Container image tag reused after in-place patch, showing old SoftwareVersion
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely below the fixed line (v4.4.0 / 3.30.0 / 2.32.0 / 0.275.0) and whether the host is internet-facing. 2) Contain: For internet-facing instances that cannot be patched immediately, disable the affected bidder adapters (advisory workaround) and add an egress deny to 169.254.169.254 + RFC1918. 3) Hunt: Correlate each vulnerable host against the SSRF egress detection (UC1) to see whether exploitation has already been attempted; prioritise patch to v4.4.0.

Ruflo MCP Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Run Commands and Poison AI Memory

The Hacker News
2026-07-29 9 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a maximum-severity security flaw in Ruflo, an open-source agent meta-harness for Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-59726 (CVSS score: 10.0), impacts all versions of the project before version 3.16.3. It has been codenamed RufRoot by Noma Security's

Unauthenticated Ruflo MCP RCE: POST /mcp tools/call ruflo__terminal_execute AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-59726 (RufRoot) exploit request: an unauthenticated HTTP POST to the Ruflo MCP bridge on port 3001 invoking the JSON-RPC method tools/call against the ruflo__terminal_execute tool. This is the exact single-request foothold that yields shell inside the bridge container. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim exploit from the article's curl block: POST /mcp on port 3001 with method tools/call and tool name ruflo__terminal_execute. Endpoint+method+port alone is already highly specific to Ruflo; body keyword match makes it conclusive. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty as those pipelines carry no generic reverse-proxy/WAF HTTP-body telemetry for this Linux/Docker service. Cross-checked against: • https://noma.security/blog/rufroot-the-mcp-bridge-vulnerability-that-turns-agents-into-rogue-admins-cve-2026-59726/ • https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo/security/advisories/GHSA-c4hm-4h84-2cf3 • https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo/releases/tag/v3.16.3
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Nuclei) firing the RufRoot template against inventory
  • Ruflo maintainer/developer legitimately hitting the local MCP bridge during debugging (source = loopback/127.0.0.1)
  • Automated CI health-check probing /mcp for liveness
  • Red-team engagement replaying the PoC with authorization
Suppression filter
| where not (SourceIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) and RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus","nuclei","kube-probe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and check the HTTP status - a 200/success on POST /mcp means the unauthenticated bridge answered. Pull all requests from that source IP to /mcp in the window. 2) Contain: block source IP at the perimeter, immediately firewall ports 3001 and 27017, and upgrade Ruflo to >=3.16.3 (binds bridge to loopback, gates terminal_execute, enables Mongo auth). Rotate ALL LLM provider API keys - treat as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot to the host - look for shell children of the node/bridge process (UC2), backdoor writes to /app (UC3), and injected agentdb_pattern-store entries / MongoDB tampering (UC4).

| where (Message has_any ("ruflo__terminal_execute","terminal_execute","tools/call")) or (RequestContext has_any ("ruflo__terminal_execute","terminal_execute","tools/call")) or DestinationPort == 3001
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Ruflo MCP bridge (node) spawning a shell — terminal_execute payload AIExploitation High
Detects the post-exploitation step of CVE-2026-59726: the Ruflo MCP bridge Node.js process spawning an interactive/one-off shell to run attacker commands (the article's 'id && hostname', reverse shells, or provider-API-key harvesting from container env). A node process spawning /bin/sh to read env or open a network shell is not normal bridge behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the exact parent->child relationship the exploit forces (node MCP bridge -> /bin/sh) plus the article's verbatim recon command 'id && hostname' and the described env-based provider-API-key theft (printenv/env). Node spawning an interactive shell with these strings has no benign runtime explanation for this service. Cross-checked against: • https://noma.security/blog/rufroot-the-mcp-bridge-vulnerability-that-turns-agents-into-rogue-admins-cve-2026-59726/ • https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo/security/advisories/GHSA-c4hm-4h84-2cf3
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Ruflo tool workflows that shell out to run user-authorized commands (if MCP_ENABLE_TERMINAL=true is intentionally set post-patch)
  • Container entrypoint/init scripts where node spawns sh during startup
  • Node child_process build/test steps invoking env or shell utilities in CI images
  • Ops engineer running 'docker exec' diagnostics that appear as shell under the app tree
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/entrypoint","docker-entrypoint","npm run build","npm test") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("containerd-shim","dockerd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the full ProcessCommandLine - 'id && hostname' or /dev/tcp reverse-shell = confirmed RufRoot exploitation, not a benign tool call. Grab the initiating node PID and correlate to inbound /mcp requests (UC1) in the same second. 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, kill the node bridge process, firewall 3001+27017, and rebuild the container from a clean image (backdoor may already be resident). Rotate every provider API key in the container env. 3) Hunt: enumerate all child processes of the bridge for the session, check for /app writes (UC3) and outbound C2, and review AgentDB for poisoned patterns (UC4).
