Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Install/import of compromised @joyfill 2773 beta package versions
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Node.js spawning shell/recon binaries or detached node -e loader · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Two Compromised joyfill npm Packages Run RAT When Imported Into Node.js
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Node.js modifying developer-tool modules for RAT self-reload persistence · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] RAT C2 egress to hardcoded joyfill IPs and /$/boot request paths · [LLM] Node.js resolving C2 via Tron + Binance Smart Chain dead-drop RPC · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Node.js spawning Python credential-stealer child · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Install/import of compromised @joyfill 2773 beta package versions AIDelivery High
Detects execution of npm/node referencing the hijacked @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts prerelease versions carrying the '2773' beta tag. These specific versions ship an obfuscated RAT that runs on import, so any host that installed or built against them must be treated as compromised. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete package names (@joyfill/components, @joyfill/layouts) and the unique '2773' beta tag common to all six malicious versions; the pairing is effectively zero-FP because no benign build references both tokens. Not externally cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally auditing the malicious package in a sandbox VM
  • Internal mirror/proxy pre-fetch of the version for quarantine analysis
  • Security tooling that clones the tarball to diff it (StepSecurity-style research)
  • A package-lock file merge conflict resolution that lists the string in a diff view opened by node
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually resolved/built the 2773 version (check node_modules/@joyfill and package-lock.json), not just referenced it in a diff. 2) Contain: isolate the developer workstation and CI runner; the payload runs on import so treat the box as compromised — rotate all credentials present (browser, Git/GitHub CLI, keychains). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceName for outbound to the C2 IPs, node spawning python, and modification of @vscode/deviceid / GitHub Desktop main.js.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "joyfill" and ProcessCommandLine has "2773"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "joyfill" and CommandLine has "2773"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RAT C2 egress to hardcoded joyfill IPs and /$/boot request paths AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections to the four command-and-control IPs and the distinctive HTTP request paths (/$/boot, /u/e, /u/f, /0x/js, /verify-human/, /snv) used by the joyfill RAT's Socket.IO channel and second-stage boot loader. High-fidelity IOC match. Rationale: Directly matches the article's four C2 IPs (incl. 23.27.13.43 that serves /$/boot) and the six unique request paths; these are singular IOCs with no benign use. Not externally cross-checked (article notes infra was likely taken down post-disclosure).
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/IOC validation scanners that deliberately probe the C2 IPs
  • A recycled/reassigned IP later hosting a benign service (IPs rotate)
  • Proxy logs replayed during a tabletop exercise
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a monitored subnet
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe or a detached node -e child) and confirm it correlates with a joyfill import on the same host. 2) Contain: block the four IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and pull the process for memory capture before reboot. 3) Hunt: sweep all egress logs org-wide for the same IPs/paths, and check for the blockchain resolver traffic (trongrid + bsc) that precedes the live-C2 resolution.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("166.88.134.62","23.27.13.43","198.105.127.210","23.27.202.27")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("/$/boot","/0x/js","/verify-human/","/u/e","/u/f","/snv")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("166.88.134.62","23.27.13.43","198.105.127.210","23.27.202.27")
   or RequestURL has_any ("/$/boot","/0x/js","/verify-human/","/snv")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js resolving C2 via Tron + Binance Smart Chain dead-drop RPC AICommand & Control Medium
Detects a node process contacting two or more public blockchain RPC endpoints (Tron, Aptos, BSC) used by the joyfill loader to resolve its live C2 through an on-chain transaction (eth_getTransactionByHash). A React/UI dev process reaching multiple chain RPCs is highly anomalous. Rationale: Ties the article's specific dead-drop resolver behaviour (Tron -> BSC via eth_getTransactionByHash) to the concrete RPC hosts; requiring >=2 distinct chain endpoints from a node process filters normal single-chain dApp traffic. Not externally cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate blockchain/web3 developer building a multi-chain dApp with node
  • Crypto wallet or exchange tooling that queries several RPC endpoints
  • node-based analytics service polling public chain data
  • CI job for a web3 project running integration tests against testnets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "web3" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "hardhat" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "truffle"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host has no legitimate web3/blockchain project (check package.json deps and developer role); a UI/React shop hitting Tron+BSC is a strong TP. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture the node process command line and memory; block the resolver domains if no legit web3 use. 3) Hunt: correlate the resolver window with subsequent egress to the hardcoded C2 IPs and /$/boot, and check for the python credential stealer child.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")
| summarize ChainEndpoints=make_set(RemoteUrl), Conns=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where array_length(ChainEndpoints) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")
| summarize ChainDomains=make_set(DnsQuery), Cnt=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where array_length(ChainDomains) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe) @DestinationHostname:(api.trongrid.io OR fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com OR bsc-dataseed.binance.org OR bsc-rpc.publicnode.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest (DomainName=/trongrid\.io$/i OR DomainName=/aptoslabs\.com$/i OR DomainName=/binance\.org$/i OR DomainName=/publicnode\.com$/i) ContextImageFileName=/node(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=collect([DomainName]))
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count values(All_Traffic.dest) as chain_endpoints from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest IN ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")) AND (All_Traffic.app="node.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="node.exe") by All_Traffic.src _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | eval endpoint_count=mvcount(chain_endpoints) | where endpoint_count>=2
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(All_Traffic.dest) as chain_endpoints from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest IN ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")) AND (All_Traffic.app="node.exe" OR All_Traffic.process_name="node.exe") by All_Traffic.src _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | eval endpoint_count=mvcount(chain_endpoints) | where endpoint_count>=2
Node.js modifying developer-tool modules for RAT self-reload persistence AIInstallation High
Detects node writing to the specific developer-tool files the joyfill RAT hijacks for persistence: the @vscode/deviceid module (VS Code/Cursor/Antigravity), the Discord desktop core module, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI. Persistence via these files means the RAT reloads whenever the dev tool runs. Rationale: Uses the four exact persistence targets named in the article (@vscode/deviceid, Discord core, GitHub Desktop main.js, global npm CLI) with node as the writing process — an unusual combination since these vendor files are normally only touched by their own installers. Not externally cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate VS Code / Cursor auto-update rewriting @vscode/deviceid
  • GitHub Desktop self-update replacing main.js
  • npm global self-update (npm i -g npm) rewriting npm CLI files
  • Discord client patcher (e.g. BetterDiscord) modifying core modules
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "update" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("Update.exe","GitHubDesktop.exe","Code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the modified file against a clean copy of the module and look for the injected self-reload block / '9-0135-3' marker; confirm the writer was node, not the vendor's own updater. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove the injected block or reinstall the affected dev tool, and rotate developer credentials. 3) Hunt: check for the joyfill import, the python stealer child, and C2 egress on the same host and any host sharing the developer's credentials.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\@vscode\deviceid", @"\GitHub Desktop\", @"\Discord\", @"\npm\node_modules\npm")
| where FileName endswith ".js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileCreated")
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("@vscode\\deviceid", "GitHub Desktop\\", "Discord\\", "npm\\node_modules\\npm")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Node.js Writes to Developer-Tool Modules for RAT Persistence

description: Detects node modifying @vscode/deviceid, Discord core, GitHub Desktop main.js, or the global npm CLI to persist the joyfill RAT

#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/node(\.exe)?$/i (TargetFileName=/@vscode.deviceid/i OR TargetFileName=/GitHub Desktop/i OR TargetFileName=/npm.node_modules.npm/i OR TargetFileName=/discord.*core/i) TargetFileName=/\.js$/i

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*@vscode?deviceid*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*GitHub Desktop*main.js" OR Filesystem.file_path="*npm?node_modules?npm*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*discord*core*") AND Filesystem.process_name="node.exe" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Node.js spawning shell/recon binaries or detached node -e loader AIExploitation Medium
Detects the joyfill RAT's execution stage: a node process spawning command interpreters or system-recon tools, or launching a detached 'node -e' child (the second-stage boot loader). This surfaces the RAT's ss_eval arbitrary-command capability and host enumeration. Rationale: Grounds the article's ss_eval RAT verb and the explicitly described detached 'node -e' second-stage loader in a parent(node)->child(interpreter/recon) process-tree pivot; the node -e clause targets the exact loader behaviour the report detonated. Not externally cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / native module builds invoking cmd.exe or powershell during npm install
  • Build scripts (webpack, npm run) legitimately shelling out to system tools
  • Electron dev tooling spawning node -e helper processes
  • CI pipelines running node-driven test harnesses that call ipconfig/netstat for diagnostics
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("webpack","npm-cli.js run","rebuild")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — recon tools (whoami/systeminfo) or a node -e with an obfuscated/base64 body are strong TPs; benign builds show recognisable build-tool args. 2) Contain: isolate the host and suspend the node process tree; capture the node -e argument for analysis. 3) Hunt: correlate with joyfill import, blockchain resolver, C2 egress, and python stealer on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe","tasklist.exe","sh","bash")
   or (FileName in~ ("node.exe","node") and ProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe","tasklist.exe")
   or (TargetProcessName has "node" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Node.js Spawns Shell Recon Tools or Detached node -e Loader
id: c1a9f6d3-8e42-4b70-a15c-3d9e0b2f7c88
description: Detects the joyfill RAT execution stage where node spawns interpreters/recon tools or a detached node -e second stage
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

detection:

      - '\systeminfo.exe'
      - '\ipconfig.exe'
      - '\netstat.exe'

level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\whoami.exe OR *\systeminfo.exe OR *\ipconfig.exe OR *\netstat.exe OR *\tasklist.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/node(\.exe)?$/i (ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|whoami|systeminfo|ipconfig|netstat|tasklist)\.exe$/i OR (ImageFileName=/node(\.exe)?$/i CommandLine=/ -e /))

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="node.exe" AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe","tasklist.exe","sh","bash") OR Processes.process="*node* -e *") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="node.exe" AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","netstat.exe","tasklist.exe","sh","bash") OR Processes.process="*node* -e *") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Node.js spawning Python credential-stealer child AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a node process launching a Python interpreter — the joyfill RAT stages a Python infostealer that collects browser data, extension wallets/password managers, Git/GitHub CLI creds and OS keychains. A React/UI library (@joyfill) has no legitimate reason to invoke Python, making this a high-signal credential-access pivot. Rationale: Maps the article's explicit 'stages a Python credential stealer' behaviour to a node->python parent/child relationship; because @joyfill is a JS/React library with no Python build dependency, node spawning python is a rare, high-fidelity signal. Not externally cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / native addon builds invoking python for build steps
  • A polyglot repo where node tooling orchestrates python data scripts
  • ML/AI dev workstation where node front-end shells out to python backends
  • Electron apps bundling python helpers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node-gyp" and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","gyp","setup.py build","rebuild")
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the python command line and whether the project legitimately depends on python (node-gyp build vs. an opaque/one-off script targeting browser profile paths). 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately — assume browser, Git/GitHub, keychain and wallet credentials are stolen; force-rotate them and revoke sessions/tokens. 3) Hunt: look for the encrypted archive upload to the C2 IPs, the joyfill import, and persistence writes to dev-tool modules on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,

let BadIPs     = dynamic(["166.88.134.62", "23.27.13.43", "198.105.127.210", "23.27.202.27"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["api.trongrid.io", "fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com", "bsc-dataseed.binance.org", "bsc-rpc.publicnode.com"]);

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

            - '\Program Files\'

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79")

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "2258284d65f63829bd67eaba01ef6f1ada2f593f9bbe41678b2df360bd90d3df", "1e8538c6e0563d50da0f2e097e979ebd5294ce1defe01d0b9fe361ba3bed1898", "e7d582b98ca80690883175470e96f703ef6dc497", "12f35b1081b17d21815b35feb57ab03d02482116", "820fa07a7328b6cf2b417078e103721d4d8f2e79"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

Vulnerable @hypequery/clickhouse dependency present (< 2.0.2, CVE-2026-54658) AIExploitation High
Inventories hosts/containers where the @hypequery/clickhouse npm package is installed (node_modules/@hypequery/clickhouse) or flagged by TVM for CVE-2026-54658. This is the first-line exposure hunt for the SQL-injection-in-escapeValue advisory before any exploitation is attempted. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable package coordinate (@hypequery/clickhouse) and node_modules path plus the assigned CVE-2026-54658; a package-present hunt is the highest-confidence exposure signal for a dependency advisory with no IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/advisories/
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev/CI build agents that legitimately install the package as part of the app
  • Hosts already upgraded to 2.0.2+ (file-presence check can't read the installed version)
  • npm/yarn offline mirror or cache directories holding the tarball
  • Monorepos with multiple hoisted copies of the package inflating FileCount
  • Container base-image scanning sandboxes that pull all dependency versions
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "2.0.2" and toint(split(SoftwareVersion, ".")[0]) < 2
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each host, confirm the installed version — read package.json/package-lock.json under @hypequery/clickhouse and check whether it is < 2.0.2; cross-reference the TVM CveId hit. Step 2 (contain): For confirmed <2.0.2 on internet-facing/user-facing services, prioritise `npm install @hypequery/clickhouse@2.0.2` (or later) and redeploy; there is no runtime workaround per the advisory. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC-2/UC-3 web and DB query-log detections for that host to determine whether the injection was already attempted before patching.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"@hypequery\clickhouse", "@hypequery/clickhouse")
| summarize FileCount = count(), FoldersSeen = make_set(FolderPath, 25), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, DeviceId
| order by LastSeen desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId == "CVE-2026-54658"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc

@hypequery/clickhouse SQLi: backslash-quote escape bypass in web/API request parameters AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP/WAF request parameters that carry the CVE-2026-54658 exploitation primitive — a value with a trailing backslash immediately preceding a single quote (raw \' or URL-encoded %5C%27) — combined with SQL follow-on keywords. This is the on-the-wire signature of an attacker escaping the closing quote emitted by escapeValue(). Rationale: Encodes the article's precise exploitation mechanic — 'trailing backslash to escape the closing quote' — as a backslash-quote (\' / %5C%27) token gated by SQL keywords, so it fires on the injection attempt rather than a generic SQLi template. Requires the app to sit behind a WAF/reverse-proxy that logs request payloads; Defender has no web-log table (left empty). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners (Burp/ZAP/Nuclei/Acunetix) running authorised SQLi test payloads
  • Legitimate query strings containing Windows paths ending in a backslash before a quoted value
  • Analytics dashboards passing ClickHouse system.* table names in URL filters
  • Encoded file paths in file-manager apps producing %5C sequences
  • Pen-test engagements from known internal source IPs
Suppression filter
| where DestinationHostName !has_any ("scanner", "appsec", "pentest") and SourceIP !in ("10.10.10.0")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Decode the RequestURL/Payload and confirm the backslash precedes the string-terminating quote (not a legitimate escaped path); note SourceIP, destination host and whether the target app depends on @hypequery/clickhouse (UC-1). Step 2 (contain): Block the SourceIP at the WAF and, if the target is <2.0.2, take the endpoint out of rotation / apply the 2.0.2 upgrade. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate the same SourceIP across other parameters/endpoints and pivot to UC-3/UC-4 on the backend DB host to confirm whether the injected SQL actually executed.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| extend Payload = strcat(tostring(RequestURL), " ", tostring(RequestContext), " ", tostring(Message))
| where Payload matches regex @"(?i)(\\'|%5c%27)"
| where Payload has_any ("UNION", "SELECT", "OR 1=1", "OR%201=1", " OR ", "--", "/*", "system.", "FROM system")
| where isempty(SourceUserName) or SourceUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, Payload
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SQL injection backslash-quote escape in web request (CVE-2026-54658 primitive)
id: 7b2c8f14-3d6a-4e29-9f5b-8a1c0e7d6b52

references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  escape:
    c-uri-query|contains:
      - "\\'"
      - '%5C%27'
      - '%5c%27'
  sqlkw:
    c-uri-query|contains:
      - 'UNION'
      - 'SELECT'
      - 'OR 1=1'
      - 'OR%201=1'
      - '--'
      - 'system.'
  condition: escape and sqlkw
level: high
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*%5C%27*" OR Web.url="*%5c%27*" OR Web.url="*\\'*") AND (Web.url="*UNION*" OR Web.url="*SELECT*" OR Web.url="*OR%201=1*" OR Web.url="*--*" OR Web.url="*system.*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*%5C%27*" OR Web.url="*%5c%27*" OR Web.url="*\\'*") AND (Web.url="*UNION*" OR Web.url="*SELECT*" OR Web.url="*OR%201=1*" OR Web.url="*--*" OR Web.url="*system.*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_method Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - lastTime
ClickHouse query_log shows injected SQL from @hypequery escapeValue bypass AIExploitation Medium
Hunts ClickHouse server/query logs (shipped via Syslog) for statements containing the backslash-quote escape artifact together with injection follow-on SQL (UNION, OR 1=1, access to system.* tables). This is where CVE-2026-54658 exploitation becomes visible as actually-executed arbitrary SQL on the database tier. Rationale: Targets the backend evidence of 'arbitrary SQL execution' by matching the same backslash-quote artifact plus injection keywords in ClickHouse query logs; higher fidelity than the web-edge UC because it confirms the statement reached and parsed on the DB. Depends on ClickHouse logs being forwarded to Syslog/Datadog (noted); no Defender equivalent. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate application queries that read from ClickHouse system.* tables (dashboards, monitoring)
  • Data-migration or admin scripts using UNION for legitimate merges
  • String literals in analytics data that naturally contain \' sequences
  • Query replay from load-testing tools
  • Backup/ETL jobs enumerating system.parts or system.tables
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full matching query and its originating user/client from query_log; determine whether the backslash-quote breaks out of a parameter string vs. appearing inside a legitimate literal. Step 2 (contain): If injection is confirmed, revoke the DB user/API credential the app uses, isolate the app host, and force the 2.0.2 upgrade. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all queries from the same client_id/initial_user around the event for data-exfiltration (SELECT from sensitive tables), and correlate back to the UC-2 web request that delivered the payload.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where ProcessName has "clickhouse" or SyslogMessage has "clickhouse"
| where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)(\\'|%5c%27)"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("UNION", "OR 1=1", " OR ", "system.", "FROM system", "--", "/*")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog @process.name:clickhouse-server (*\\'* OR *%5c%27*) AND (*UNION* OR *"OR 1=1"* OR *system.* OR *"FROM system"*)
APPLICATION
index=* (sourcetype=clickhouse OR sourcetype=clickhouse:query_log OR source="*clickhouse-server*")
| regex _raw="(?i)(\\'|%5c%27)"
| search ("UNION" OR "OR 1=1" OR " OR 1=1" OR "system." OR "FROM system" OR "--")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(host) as hosts by _raw
| sort - count
ClickHouse SQL syntax-error spike from @hypequery/clickhouse injection probing AIExploitation Low
Threshold hunt for a burst of ClickHouse SYNTAX_ERROR (Code: 62) / escapeValue-related exceptions on an application host, indicating an attacker iterating backslash-quote payloads against CVE-2026-54658 before a working injection lands. Failed injection attempts leave parser errors even when the successful one does not. Rationale: Names the article's escapeValue() function and the vulnerable package, plus ClickHouse's SYNTAX_ERROR code (62) that malformed injection payloads trigger; an error-rate spike is a cheap early-warning for injection fuzzing that the pattern-match UCs may miss when payloads are encoded. Telemetry depends on app/DB error logs reaching Syslog/Datadog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcc-39rp-hh9p • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-54658
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Buggy application release emitting genuine malformed queries after a deploy
  • Developer/analyst ad-hoc query session with typos against the same ClickHouse
  • Schema-migration window where queries reference not-yet-created columns
  • BI tool generating invalid SQL for unsupported functions
  • Load/chaos testing that intentionally sends malformed statements
Suppression filter
| where Sample !has_any ("migration", "ALTER TABLE", "CREATE TABLE")
Response runbook

Step 2 (contain): If external and injection-shaped, block the source at the WAF, revoke the app's DB credential, and schedule the 2.0.2 upgrade. Step 3 (hunt): Look for one successful (non-error) query from the same client immediately after the error burst (the payload that worked) and pivot to UC-3 to assess data access.

goshs WebDAV --no-delete bypass: blocked DELETE followed by successful MOVE on same path AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-64863 exploit signature where an attacker probes the --no-delete restriction (DELETE returns 403) and then destroys the same resource via the WebDAV MOVE verb (201 Created / 204 No Content). The 403-then-2xx pairing on an identical URL within a short window is the bypass fingerprint, not generic WebDAV usage. Rationale: Uses the article's exact control-vs-bypass pairing: DELETE=403 (blocked by --no-delete) then MOVE=201/204 (RemoveAll/rename succeeds). Correlating both on the same URL from the same source removes benign WebDAV MOVE traffic, which never co-occurs with a just-refused DELETE on the identical path. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://cve.threatint.com/CVE/CVE-2026-64863
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A WebDAV sync client (Finder/Explorer) that retries a delete as a rename after a transient 403 for reasons unrelated to policy
  • Automated backup tooling that first attempts DELETE, is denied, and falls back to MOVE-to-archive on the same object
  • Load/security scanners (e.g. Nessus WebDAV checks) exercising both verbs against the same test path
  • Reverse proxy that rewrites and duplicates request lines, double-logging one client action as two verbs
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target server is goshs (<= v2.1.3) — check the response Server header 'goshs/...' and whether it was launched with '-w --no-delete'; pull the full request sequence for the src IP against the affected URL. 2) Contain: block the src IP at the WAF/proxy and stop/upgrade the goshs instance to v2.1.4 (or drop WebDAV write verbs MOVE/COPY at the proxy) so the --no-delete boundary is actually enforced. 3) Hunt: enumerate every MOVE 201/204 from that src across all served paths to scope which artefacts were renamed away or overwritten, and check file integrity of the served directory against a known-good manifest.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csMethod in ("DELETE","MOVE")
| extend DeleteBlocked = iff(csMethod == "DELETE" and scStatus == 403, 1, 0)
| extend MoveSuccess = iff(csMethod == "MOVE" and scStatus in (201, 204), 1, 0)
| where DeleteBlocked == 1 or MoveSuccess == 1
| summarize DeleteBlocked = sum(DeleteBlocked), MoveSuccess = sum(MoveSuccess), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Statuses = make_set(scStatus) by cIP, csUriStem, Computer, sSiteName
| where DeleteBlocked > 0 and MoveSuccess > 0
| order by LastSeen desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where (Web.http_method="DELETE" AND Web.status=403) OR (Web.http_method="MOVE" AND Web.status IN (201,204)) by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.dest_port, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.status, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval delete_blocked=if(http_method=="DELETE" AND status=="403",1,0)
| eval move_success=if(http_method=="MOVE" AND (status=="201" OR status=="204"),1,0)
| stats sum(delete_blocked) as delete_blocked, sum(move_success) as move_success, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(status) as statuses by src, dest, dest_port, url
| where delete_blocked>0 AND move_success>0
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.http_method="DELETE" AND Web.status=403) OR (Web.http_method="MOVE" AND Web.status IN (201,204)) by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.dest_port, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.status, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval delete_blocked=if(http_method=="DELETE" AND status=="403",1,0)
| eval move_success=if(http_method=="MOVE" AND (status=="201" OR status=="204"),1,0)
| stats sum(delete_blocked) as delete_blocked, sum(move_success) as move_success, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(status) as statuses by src, dest, dest_port, url
| where delete_blocked>0 AND move_success>0
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
WebDAV MOVE/COPY write-verb succeeds against goshs artifact server (Overwrite:T destination clobber) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces successful WebDAV MOVE/COPY verbs (201/204) against an exposed goshs file server, the mechanism CVE-2026-64863 abuses to rename-away or, with the 'Overwrite: T' header, RemoveAll and overwrite existing files under --no-delete. MOVE/COPY are rare in normal artifact-download traffic, so a success is a high-signal exploitation candidate. Rationale: Keys on the article's exploitation primitive — the WebDAV MOVE/COPY verbs returning 201/204 — plus the 'Overwrite: T' header called out as the RemoveAll trigger (grep RequestContext/Message where the WAF logs headers). MOVE/COPY are near-absent in legitimate file-download workloads, so a success against a goshs host is worth a hunt even without correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-50138/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDAV clients (Finder, Windows Explorer, Cyberduck) renaming files on a genuinely writable goshs share (no --no-delete set)
  • CI/CD or backup jobs that use MOVE to atomically publish artifacts into the served directory
  • SharePoint/Nextcloud or other WebDAV appliances behind the same WAF that legitimately use MOVE/COPY
  • Web content-management operations issuing COPY for versioning
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is a goshs instance and whether it runs with --no-delete/--read-only; inspect the request for a 'Destination:' and 'Overwrite: T' header (header-logging WAFs) that indicates intent to clobber an existing file. 2) Contain: strip MOVE/COPY at the proxy for that vhost and upgrade goshs to v2.1.4; restrict the WebDAV port to trusted source ranges. 3) Hunt: pivot on the src IP to list all MOVE/COPY targets and any preceding blocked DELETE (see companion rule) to determine which served files were destroyed or overwritten.

| where RequestMethod in ("MOVE", "COPY")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

goshs process deletes or renames served files while launched with --no-delete (impact confirmation) AIActions on Objectives High
Confirms real data loss from CVE-2026-64863 on the host: a goshs process removing or renaming files (os.Rename / RemoveAll) even though it was started with --no-delete. Under that flag goshs should never delete anything, so any goshs-initiated file delete/rename event is a direct policy violation and proof the WebDAV MOVE bypass fired. Rationale: Combines the article's process (goshs) with its stated invariant (--no-delete means no deletion) — so a goshs-initiated FileDeleted/FileRenamed with '--no-delete' on the command line is a definitional bypass with essentially no benign explanation. This is the on-host impact confirmation for the HTTP-layer rules. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/goshs.de/goshs/v2/CVE-2026-64863/ • https://github.com/goshs-labs/goshs/releases
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • An operator manually deleting files in the served directory with another tool (would not show goshs as the initiating process)
  • goshs launched without --no-delete performing intended deletes (excluded by the --no-delete command-line filter)
  • Log-rotation or the goshs binary being self-updated/replaced on disk (rename of the binary rather than served content)
Suppression filter
// Defender: exclude self-update/binary replacement and keep only served-content paths
| where not (FileName endswith "goshs" or FileName endswith "goshs.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine to confirm --no-delete/--webdav were set, and capture FolderPath/PreviousFolderPath to identify exactly which served file was renamed or removed. 2) Contain: stop the goshs service and upgrade to v2.1.4 (or remove WebDAV); restore the affected file(s) from backup, as MOVE/RemoveAll destroys the original content. 3) Hunt: correlate the file event timestamp back to the WebDAV access log for the matching MOVE 201/204 and its source IP to attribute the actor, and review whether other files in the same directory disappeared in the same window.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "goshs"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted", "FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, PreviousFolderPath, PreviousFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where ActingProcessName has "goshs"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--no-delete"
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted", "FileRenamed")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable goshs SFTP launch: empty-credential basic-auth (-b 'user:' / ':pass') with -sftp and no -fkf AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact vulnerable configuration for CVE-2026-62325 / CVE-2026-40884: a goshs process started with -sftp and a -b basic-auth string that has an empty username or empty password, and without -fkf (public-key). This combination disables the SFTP PasswordHandler (gliderlabs/ssh sets NoClientAuth=true), exposing unauthenticated file read/write/delete/rename. Article-specific because it keys on the literal goshs binary and its -b/-sftp/-fkf flag semantics, not a generic SSH check. Rationale: Uses the article's literal vulnerable invocation `goshs -b 'admin:' -sftp` and the flag logic (`-b` empty-side + `-sftp` + absence of `-fkf`) that produces NoClientAuth=true. The empty-credential regex catches both the CVE-2026-62325 empty-password variant and the CVE-2026-40884 empty-username variant. Cross-checked against the SentinelOne CVE-2026-40884 entry and the GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv GitLab advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40884/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm
ATT&CKT1190 T1021.004 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pentester/red-team intentionally running goshs as a throwaway file server on an engagement host
  • CTF or lab boxes where goshs is deliberately started with weak auth for training
  • Automation/scripts that pass -b with a trailing colon by mistake but on an internal-only isolated host
  • Security researcher reproducing the CVE in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("pentest", "redteam", "ctf", "lab") and InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("pentest", "redteam"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the exact `-b` value and whether `-fkf` is absent; identify the listening port and whether the host is internet-facing (check DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing / firewall NAT). 2) CONTAIN: Kill the goshs process and block the SFTP listener port at the host firewall; if internet-facing, treat as actively exploitable and isolate the host. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2/UC3 — enumerate inbound SFTP connections this goshs PID accepted and every file it read/wrote/deleted; determine data exposure and whether any remote client IP is external.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName has "goshs" or ProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-sftp"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-b"
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "-fkf"
// empty-password ( user: ) or empty-username ( :pass ) in the -b basic-auth string
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-b\s+['""]?([^\s'"":]+:(?:['""]|\s|$)|:[^\s'""]+)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where ActingProcessName has "goshs" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "goshs"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "-sftp"

title: Vulnerable goshs SFTP Launch With Empty-Credential Basic Auth (CVE-2026-62325)
id: 2f7c1e8a-4b6d-4c9a-9f21-8d3b7a6e0c14
description: Detects goshs started with -sftp and a -b basic-auth string with an empty username or empty password and no -fkf, disabling the SFTP password handler and exposing unauthenticated file access.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/patrickhener/goshs/GHSA-c29w-qq4m-2gcv/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1021.004
  - attack.t1133
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|contains: 'goshs'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '-sftp'
      - '-b'
  selection_emptycred:
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)-b\s+[''"]?([^\s''":]+:([''"]|\s|$)|:[^\s''"]+)'
  filter_pubkey:
    CommandLine|contains: '-fkf'
  condition: selection_img and selection_flags and selection_emptycred and not filter_pubkey
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:*goshs* @process.command_line:*\-sftp* @process.command_line:*\-b* -@process.command_line:*\-fkf*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/goshs(\.exe)?$/i
| CommandLine=/-sftp/i
| CommandLine=/-b\s+['"]?([^\s'":]+:(['"]|\s|$)|:[^\s'"]+)/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/-fkf/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

goshs process accepting inbound SFTP/SSH connections (exposed file server) AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces a goshs binary acting as an SFTP/SSH server by flagging inbound connections it accepts. Complements the process-launch detection by catching live exploitation and any goshs listener whose launch telemetry was missed. Article-specific: keys on the goshs process as the network-listening initiator rather than a generic SSH port. Rationale: Ties the network-listener behaviour to the specific goshs binary named throughout the article (impact: 'Unauthenticated SFTP file access'), so it flags exposure and live client connections rather than any SSH traffic. RemoteIPType surfaces external clients for prioritisation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40884/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm

File read/write/delete/rename performed by a goshs process (SFTP data access) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the actual file-system impact of the goshs SFTP bypass by surfacing file create/modify/delete/rename operations whose initiating process is goshs. This is the collection/impact stage the auth bypass enables (read, write, delete, rename per the article). Article-specific: pivots on goshs as the file-operation initiator, not a generic file-write rule. Rationale: Directly targets the article's stated impact ('Unauthenticated SFTP file access (read, write, delete, rename)') by attributing file operations to the goshs process. High value when correlated with UC1's vulnerable-launch alert to quantify what data was exposed. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rjrw-mjq6-hpmm • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40884/

Endpoint traffic to cubepilot.org during 24 Jul 2026 DNS-hijack / AiTM window AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for any host that resolved or connected to cubepilot.org or its subdomains (portal, discuss/forum, docs) during the 24 July 2026 DNS-hijack window, when traffic was redirected to attacker infrastructure holding fraudulent TLS certs. Any credentials entered on those services may have been captured. Surfaces the resolved RemoteIP so an analyst can identify the attacker-controlled address. Rationale: Anchors on the exact victim domain (cubepilot.org and subdomains portal/discuss/docs confirmed on CubePilot's own security notice) bounded to the 24 Jul 2026 hijack window; make_set on RemoteIP/DnsResponseName surfaces the attacker-controlled resolution so no attacker IP needs to be hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/
ATT&CKT1557 T1584.002 T1056.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineer legitimately browsing docs.cubepilot.org or the forum during the window without entering credentials
  • DNS query that resolved to the legitimate host if it occurred outside the actual redirection minutes (control was regained the same day)
  • Automated firmware/version-check services polling cubepilot.org on a schedule
  • CI/CD or package tooling pulling from CubePilot repos
  • Security team already testing/validating the domain post-incident
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ResolvedIPs for each hit; any answer outside CubePilot's normal hosting ASN during 24 Jul is the attacker endpoint — pivot all hosts sharing that IP. 2) Contain: force password reset for any user who authenticated to portal/forum/docs on 24 Jul (creds may be captured) and revoke active sessions; block the attacker IP. 3) Hunt: search auth logs for the affected users signing in from anomalous IPs post-24 Jul, and check for password reuse alerts across SSO/VPN/email.

CubePilot firmware/file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 Jul 2026 (possible tampered supply chain) AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for firmware images or any file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 July 2026 — the window CubePilot flagged as unverified pending checksum review. Files pulled while attacker infrastructure served the domain may be trojanised; this surfaces the filenames and SHA256 so analysts can quarantine and compare against CubePilot's confirmed-good hashes before any flashing. Rationale: Keys on FileOriginUrl containing cubepilot.org bounded to the exact 24-25 Jul window CubePilot said needs checksum verification; projecting SHA256/FileName lets an analyst diff against confirmed-good firmware hashes. Datadog/Falcon left blank because Sysmon EID11 and FDR FileWritten do not carry the download-origin URL needed to tie a firmware file back to cubepilot.org. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

OpenAI models used Artifactory zero-days to escape to the internet

BleepingComputer
2026-07-28 6 use cases 1 technique 6 kill-chain phases detected

JFrog has confirmed that OpenAI models exploited zero-day vulnerabilities in self-hosted Artifactory servers to help escape an isolated testing environment and gain access to the internet before attacking Hugging Face. [...]

CVEsCVE-2026-65921 CVE-2026-65923 CVE-2026-65924 CVE-2026-65925 CVE-2026-66014 CVE-2026-66015 CVE-2026-65617 CVE-2026-66018
ATT&CKT1190
